key_terms.meaning: Column in which longitudinal bars are held by rectangular or circular lateral ties; the ties restrain buckling of the bars and give visible warning before failure.
Column with continuous helical reinforcement in place of ties; the spiral confines the concrete core, so the axial capacity is the core capacity plus the spiral contribution.
Clear distance between lateral supports, or between the floor and the soffit of the beam resting on the column, in mm.
l<sub>e</sub> = k × L, where k depends on end restraint and on whether the frame is braced; it is the length used in the slenderness ratio.
λ = l<sub>e</sub>/i for any section (i = radius of gyration); for a rectangular section l<sub>e</sub>/D is used, and the column is short when l<sub>e</sub>/D ≤ 12 and l<sub>e</sub>/b ≤ 12.
Column with small slenderness, where second-order moments are neglected and the design is governed by material strength alone.
Column with large slenderness, where the design must add an additional moment for the lateral deflection under load.
e<sub>min</sub> = L/500 + D/30, never less than 20 mm, where L is the unsupported length and D the lateral dimension in that direction.
P<sub>u</sub> = 1.5 × service axial load, in kN, for limit state design under combined dead and live load.
Column steel must be 0.8% to 6% of the gross area (1–2% in practice); ties at pitch ≤ least lateral dimension, ≤ 16 × smallest bar diameter and ≤ 300 mm.
Curve of P<sub>u</sub> against M<sub>u</sub> that encloses every safe combination of axial load and moment for a section; the design point must lie inside it.

(M<sub>ux</sub>/M<sub>ux1</sub>)<sup>αn</sup> + (M<sub>uy</sub>/M<sub>uy1</sub>)<sup>αn</sup> ≤ 1, with αn = 1.0 when P<sub>u</sub>/P<sub>uz</sub> ≤ 0.2, 2.0 when ≥ 0.8, linear between; P<sub>uz</sub> is the pure axial capacity.
q = total load incl. self-weight of footing ÷ area of footing, in kN/m², which must not exceed the safe bearing capacity of the soil.

key_terms.term: One-way shear section in a footing
key_terms.meaning: Critical section at distance d from the face of the wall or column, where the footing acts as a cantilever slab of width 1 m in a wall footing.

Shear on the perimeter at d/2 from the column face; τ<sub>v</sub> = V<sub>u</sub>/(b<sub>0</sub>d) must be ≤ k<sub>s</sub> × 0.25√f<sub>ck</sub>, with b<sub>0</sub> the perimeter and k<sub>s</sub> = 0.5 + β<sub>c</sub> ≤ 1.0.
The footing area is proportioned so its centroid lies under the resultant of the two column loads; then the soil pressure is uniform.
The vertical cantilever wall of a retaining wall that retains the soil and transfers earth pressure to the base slab.
The part of the base slab behind the stem, under the retained soil; soil weight on the heel gives the main resisting moment against overturning.
The part of the base slab in front of the stem; it is designed as a cantilever for the upward soil pressure and adds a small restoring moment.
Design and detailing that keep crack width small (low steel stress, close spacing of small bars, minimum cover), so the tank does not leak and the steel does not corrode.

takeaways: A column is short or slender by its slenderness ratio l<sub>e</sub>/D, not by its height alone; the end conditions fix l<sub>e</sub> through k.

For a short axially loaded column, choose the steel percentage so that 0.4f<sub>ck</sub>A<sub>c</sub> + 0.67f<sub>y</sub>A<sub>sc</sub> is at least P<sub>u</sub>, then provide ties at the codal pitch.
A column with moment is safe when its (P<sub>u</sub>, M<sub>u</sub>) point lies inside the interaction diagram; biaxial bending uses the two-axis interaction check.
A wall footing gets its width from the soil bearing pressure and its depth from bending and one-way shear at the section d from the wall face.
An isolated footing is sized by bearing pressure and its depth is usually fixed by punching shear, not by bending.

A combined footing for two columns is first made statically neutral by putting its centroid under the resultant load, then designed as a beam in the long direction and as a cantilever in the transverse direction.
A cantilever retaining wall must first pass the three stability checks — overturning, sliding and bearing — and only then are the stem, heel and toe designed as cantilevers.
In a water tank, crack control and durability can decide the thickness and steel just as much as strength does.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit almost always ask for a full design with checks — a short column, a footing, or a retaining wall — so the marks sit in the correct load calculation, the codal checks in the right order, and the neat reinforcement sketch.

bank.q: Classify reinforced concrete columns. Explain tied and spiral columns, short and slender columns, and braced and unbraced columns, with a neat sketch of each lateral reinforcement type.
outline: Tied vs spiral: type of lateral steel, confinement effect, warning before failure, ductility
Short vs slender by l<sub>e</sub>/D ≤ 12 (and l<sub>e</sub>/b ≤ 12)
Braced vs unbraced: relative sway at ends, effect on k and hence l<sub>e</sub>
Sketch showing ties, helix, longitudinal bars, cover

bank.q: Define effective length and slenderness ratio. Explain how end conditions change the value of k, and why minimum eccentricity is prescribed even for an 'axially loaded' column.
outline: l<sub>e</sub> = kL with k values for fixed, hinged and free ends
λ = l<sub>e</sub>/i and the l<sub>e</sub>/D limit of 12
Practical columns are never perfectly axial: accidental eccentricity from construction tolerance
e<sub>min</sub> = L/500 + D/30 ≥ 20 mm

bank.q: Explain the shape of the interaction diagram of a rectangular column. Mark the pure compression point, the balanced point and the pure bending point, and state where the design point of a typical building column lies.
outline: Axes P<sub>u</sub> and M<sub>u</sub>; the curve is the boundary of safety
Pure compression point (P<sub>uz</sub>, 0) and pure bending point (0, M<sub>u0</sub>)
Balanced point where concrete and steel reach limiting strain together
Region above balanced point is compression-controlled, below is tension-controlled
Typical column lies near the top, at low M<sub>u</sub> relative to P<sub>u</sub>

bank.q: Describe the design of a wall footing step by step: proportioning for bearing, bending at the face of the wall, one-way shear, and distribution steel.
outline: Take 1 m length of wall; width = load per metre ÷ safe bearing capacity
Thickness from bending moment at the wall face, then checked for shear at d from the face
Minimum thickness for the cantilever projection
Distribution steel at right angles, minimum percentage, and a levelling course of lean concrete

bank.q: Design a short square tied column to carry a factored axial load of 1500 kN using M25 concrete and Fe415 steel. Give the section, the longitudinal bars and the ties, with a sketch.
outline: P<sub>u</sub> = 0.4f<sub>ck</sub>A<sub>c</sub> + 0.67f<sub>y</sub>A<sub>sc</sub>
Assume 1% steel, solve for gross area, round up to a practical size (e.g. 400 × 400 mm)
Check steel percentage between 0.8% and 6%
Tie diameter ≥ quarter of the largest bar and ≥ 6 mm; pitch ≤ least lateral dimension, ≤ 16φ, ≤ 300 mm
Sketch with cover, bar arrangement and tie spacing

bank.q: A 230 mm brick wall carries a factored load of 200 kN per metre run. Design a suitable wall footing for a safe bearing capacity of 200 kN/m², using M20 concrete and Fe415 steel.
outline: Width = 200/200 = 1.0 m plus allowance for self-weight of footing
Projection on each side of the wall and the bending moment at the wall face
Depth from M<sub>u</sub> and then the one-way shear check at d from the face
Area of steel in the short direction, minimum steel and spacing
Distribution steel in the long direction

bank.q: Design a square isolated footing for a column of 400 × 400 mm carrying a factored load of 1200 kN, safe bearing capacity 180 kN/m², M25 concrete and Fe415 steel. Check one-way shear and punching shear.
outline: Size the footing for service load plus self-weight against bearing capacity
Net upward soil pressure in kN/m²
Bending moment at the column face in both directions and steel area
One-way shear at d from the face
Punching shear on the perimeter at d/2; τ<sub>v</sub> ≤ k<sub>s</sub>·0.25√f<sub>ck</sub>
Development length, cover and sketch

bank.q: A column is subjected to a factored axial load with moments about both axes. Explain the complete design check, including how M<sub>ux1</sub> and M<sub>uy1</sub> are obtained and how P<sub>uz</sub> is computed.
outline: Get M<sub>ux1</sub> for the given P<sub>u</sub> from the interaction chart or from first principles
Compute P<sub>uz</sub> = 0.45f<sub>ck</sub>A<sub>g</sub> + 0.75f<sub>y</sub>A<sub>sc</sub>
Find αn from P<sub>u</sub>/P<sub>uz</sub>
Check (M<sub>ux</sub>/M<sub>ux1</sub>)<sup>αn</sup> + (M<sub>uy</sub>/M<sub>uy1</sub>)<sup>αn</sup> ≤ 1
Revise the section or the steel if the check fails

bank.q: Two columns carry factored loads of 800 kN and 1200 kN, 4 m apart centre to centre. Proportion a combined rectangular footing so that the soil pressure is uniform, and outline the design of its longitudinal and transverse reinforcement.
outline: Find the resultant position from the heavier column
Choose a length whose centroid coincides with the resultant; width from bearing capacity
Longitudinal bending moment and shear diagrams: sagging between columns, hogging near the heavier column, cantilever beyond it
Transverse direction: each column load spreads over the local width, designed as a cantilever
Top and bottom steel, and a sketch of the layout

bank.q: Compare one-way shear and punching shear in an isolated footing. Explain the critical sections, why punching shear usually governs the depth, and what is done when the check fails.
outline: One-way shear at d from the column face on a plane across the full width
Punching shear around the perimeter at d/2; area resisting is small compared with the load
τ<sub>v</sub> = V<sub>u</sub>/(b<sub>0</sub>d) compared with k<sub>s</sub>·0.25√f<sub>ck</sub>
Remedies: increase depth, increase concrete grade, provide shear reinforcement or a pedestal

bank.q: A cantilever retaining wall is to retain 4 m of soil. Explain the stability checks against overturning, sliding and bearing failure, and state why these are done before the stem and base are designed.
outline: Active earth pressure triangular, P<sub>a</sub> = ½K<sub>a</sub>γH² acting at H/3
Restoring moment from the wall weight and the soil on the heel; factor of safety against overturning (about 1.4 to 1.55 with partial factors)
Sliding resisted by base friction (μΣV) plus passive pressure in front; check factor of safety
Bearing: e = M/ΣV must lie within B/6 so no tension; maximum pressure ≤ safe bearing capacity
Only after the base size is fixed can the stem and toe/heel moments be found

bank.q: Discuss the design of a rectangular water tank resting on the ground. Why does crack control govern, and what detailing measures keep the tank watertight?
outline: Water pressure acts on walls and base; hydrostatic pressure is triangular with depth
Permissible crack width is small in members in contact with water
Low steel stress, small diameter bars at close spacing, adequate cover
Minimum reinforcement on each face, construction joints with water bars
Strength check still needed for the empty and full conditions

bank.q: Explain how a slender column differs from a short column in behaviour and in design. Show how the additional moment arises and how the design moment is obtained.
outline: Lateral deflection under axial load creates a second-order moment P·δ
Additional moment M<sub>a</sub> = P<sub>u</sub>·e<sub>a</sub>, with e<sub>a</sub> depending on slenderness and the axial load ratio
Design moment = M<sub>u</sub> (from analysis, at least e<sub>min</sub>) plus M<sub>a</sub>
Check by the interaction diagram; reduce M<sub>a</sub> when the column is braced and the moment is small
Slender columns need more steel or a larger section than a short column for the same load

glossary.def: A column whose ends are held against relative lateral translation by bracing or by a stiff core, so k is small and l<sub>e</sub> is less than the unsupported length in the sway sense.
A column in a frame that is free to sway sideways, so the effective length is greater than the unsupported length and k exceeds 1.
i = √(I/A), in mm, used to express slenderness for non-rectangular sections.
Closed loop of steel around the longitudinal bars that prevents their buckling and confines the concrete.
Continuous spiral of steel in a circular column that confines the core and increases ductility and load capacity.
The pure axial capacity of a column section with zero moment, used to pick αn in the biaxial bending check.
The state where concrete crushing and steel yielding occur together; it marks the peak of the interaction diagram's moment axis.
The net soil pressure that can be applied with an adequate factor of safety against shear failure and settlement, in kN/m².
The factored soil reaction used to design a footing, equal to the column load divided by the footing area, in kN/m².
The section where a particular check is made: at the face for bending, at d for one-way shear, at d/2 around the column for punching.
Steel placed at right angles to the main steel to control cracking and to hold the main bars in position.
The embedded length of a bar needed to transfer its force to the concrete by bond, in mm.
Ratio of the restoring moment about the toe to the overturning moment from the earth pressure; it must exceed the codal minimum.
Ratio of the resisting horizontal force (base friction plus passive pressure) to the active thrust.
The horizontal push of soil on a wall that has moved slightly away from it, P<sub>a</sub> = ½K<sub>a</sub>γH² per metre length, in kN/m.
An extra vertical load on the soil behind a wall, such as a road or stored material, which adds to the earth pressure.
e = M/ΣV; the footing is fully in compression only when e ≤ B/6, otherwise the pressure diagram is partial.
A single footing supporting two or more columns, used when columns are close or the property line prevents separate footings.
The calculated width of a flexural crack at the tension face, in mm, limited by the code to keep the member durable and watertight.
A thin layer of lean concrete (PCC) under a footing that gives a clean, level surface for the reinforcement.
Shear on a vertical plane across the full width of a slab-like member, checked at a distance d from the support or column face.
The condition that the wall does not overturn, slide or overload the soil under the base.
